title: 嘉靖三十一年陝西鄉試錄
text:
然可誦
考試官教諭楊　批　典雅
詩人願王者之嫡嗣永享天祿而大君天下焉
蓋錫福久而治化隆天之所以厚其君者至也
詩人以是願王者之子孫亦忠愛無已之意歟
此公尸所以荅鳧鷖也蓋曰福以全盛爲難治
以永保爲貴吾王之嫡嗣脩德以基命誠心以
任賢如此則天心之眷寧容已哉是以纘承大
統而貴爲天子福莫有大焉者矣又衍茲福於
===
弗替萬有千歲不見其終窮君臨大邦而富有
四海福固無以加此矣又申爾嘏於有常於萬
斯年莫知其紀極儀譽並隆則天休滋至仰承
保定之眷有惟日不足者也何有乎限量耶治
功益懋則景福益增永綏有秩之祜有歷世皆
然者也又曷有窮已耶夫福德在君則天命可
徵也天命在君則治化可知也於焉萃百神以
爲主一人總理有以垂下國之綴旒聯四海以
爲家百辟仰承有以攝萬方之綱紀以統其同
punctuated:
然可誦。
考試官教諭楊　批：典雅。
詩人願王者之嫡嗣永享天祿，而大君天下焉。蓋錫福久而治化隆，天之所以厚其君者至也。詩人以是願王者之子孫，亦忠愛無已之意歟？此公尸所以荅鳧鷖也。蓋曰：福以全盛爲難，治以永保爲貴。吾王之嫡嗣，脩德以基命，誠心以任賢，如此則天心之眷寧容已哉？是以纘承大統而貴爲天子，福莫有大焉者矣。又衍茲福於弗替，萬有千歲，不見其終窮。君臨大邦而富有四海，福固無以加此矣。又申爾嘏於有常，於萬斯年，莫知其紀極。儀譽並隆，則天休滋至，仰承保定之眷，有惟日不足者也，何有乎限量耶？治功益懋，則景福益增，永綏有秩之祜，有歷世皆然者也，又曷有窮已耶？夫福德在君，則天命可徵也；天命在君，則治化可知也。於焉萃百神以爲主，一人總理，有以垂下國之綴旒；聯四海以爲家，百辟仰承，有以攝萬方之綱紀，以統其同
translation_en:
…and worthy of recitation.
Examiner Yang, Instructor, comments: “Classical and elegant.”
The poet wishes that the king’s legitimate heir may forever enjoy Heaven’s blessings and reign as the great ruler of all under Heaven. When blessings endure and the transforming influence of government flourishes, Heaven’s generosity toward its ruler reaches its utmost. In wishing this for the king’s descendants, does the poet not also express unending loyalty and love? This is why the ducal impersonator of the ancestors responds in “Wild Ducks” (Fu yi).
The meaning is this: blessings are difficult to attain in their fullness, and government is valued for its enduring preservation. Our king’s legitimate heir cultivates virtue to establish the foundation of his mandate and employs worthy men with sincerity. With conduct such as this, how could Heaven’s loving regard cease? Thus he succeeds to the great imperial line and holds the exalted position of Son of Heaven: no blessing could be greater. Moreover, these blessings are extended without decline; for ten thousand and a thousand years, no end to them is seen. He reigns over the great realm and possesses the wealth of all within the Four Seas: surely nothing could surpass such blessings. Moreover, your blessings are repeatedly bestowed with constancy; through ten thousand years, no one knows their utmost limit.
As his dignified bearing and reputation both flourish, Heaven’s favor comes in increasing measure. In reverently receiving its loving protection and assurance, he finds even each day insufficient: how could there be any limit? As his achievements in government become more illustrious, his great blessings increase. He forever rests securely in blessings bestowed in due order, continuing thus through successive generations: how could they ever be exhausted?
When blessings and virtue reside in the ruler, Heaven’s mandate can be verified; when Heaven’s mandate resides in the ruler, the transforming influence of his government can be understood. Thus he gathers the hundred spirits and presides over them. The One Man directs all affairs, providing the bond that holds together the subordinate states. He joins all within the Four Seas into one family; the many lords reverently receive his direction, enabling him to grasp the governing cords of the myriad regions, and thereby unite what they share…

周鑑
punctuated:
以合其異，際天遠近皆安於統馭之中，所謂建其有極者此矣，寧復有渙散者乎？以正百官，以正萬民，薄海內外盡屬其維持之內，所謂式於九圍者是矣，寧復有攜貳者乎？夫然，則君之道不以治而少弛，君之福將因此而益保矣。詩人願王者之嫡嗣而以是焉，感激之情、忠愛之意，可謂無所不用其極矣。抑論有啓以敬承繼禹之道，而夏祚以永；有成王以續文武之傳，而周室以隆。蓋守成之難，誠有係於嗣續焉者。詩人感王者鳬鷖之燕，而願其嫡嗣之賢，又必本其威儀聲譽之隆、純心用賢之要，其亦美不忘規之意歟？故曰：觀《鳬鷖》《旣醉》之歌，可以見太平有道氣象。

武丁孫子，武王靡不勝。龍旂十乘，大糦是承。邦畿千里，維民所止。肇域彼四海，四海來假。來假祁祁，景員維河。殷受命咸宜，百祿是何。

周鑑
translation_en:
…to unite their differences. Everywhere beneath Heaven, near and far, all rest secure under his rule. This is what is meant by establishing the supreme standard. Could there still be any disunity? He rectifies the hundred officials and rectifies the myriad people. Within and beyond the seas, all fall within his sustaining care. This is what is meant by serving as a model to the nine regions. Could there still be any disaffection or divided allegiance? Thus, the ruler does not relax his practice of the Way even slightly because order has been achieved, and his blessings will thereby be still more securely preserved. The poet offers these wishes for the king’s rightful heir; his gratitude and his loyal affection may be said to find their fullest expression here. Furthermore, Qi reverently continued the Way of Yu, and the Xia dynasty’s tenure endured; King Cheng continued the tradition of Wen and Wu, and the house of Zhou flourished. The difficulty of preserving an established achievement truly has much to do with succession. Moved by the king’s banquet celebrated in “Wild Ducks and Gulls” (Fu yi), the poet wishes that his rightful heir may be worthy. He necessarily grounds this wish in the heir’s distinguished deportment and reputation, and in the essentials of keeping his heart pure and employing worthy men. Does this not also convey the intention of offering praise without forgetting admonition? Thus it is said: in the songs “Wild Ducks and Gulls” and “Already Drunk” (Ji zui), one can discern the character of an age of great peace governed by the Way.

The descendants of Wu Ding all uphold the legacy of the martial king. Ten chariots with dragon banners bear the great sacrificial offerings. The royal domain extends a thousand li: here the people dwell. He first established boundaries throughout the Four Seas, and those from the Four Seas come to pay homage. They come in great multitudes; around Mount Jing flows the Yellow River. Yin received Heaven’s mandate in full fitness, and bears its hundred blessings.

Zhou Jian.

title: 嘉靖三十一年陝西鄉試錄
text:
同考試官教諭賈〔拱祿〕批　高宗中興全在武德作者多
畧之此篇得其肯綮而氣象渾厚不獨以文也錄之
考試官教諭袁〔廷椿〕批　語莊而義密商人頌德之意
正如此
考試官教諭楊〔舉〕批　典實
詩人頌賢王繼統之休以見世德之盛也蓋武
德以一天下有商世濟其盛者也然則所以承
天休者不亦至哉此亦祭祀宗廟之樂也蓋謂
一代王業不有所開固無以啓永世之休不有
===
所繼亦無以大光前之烈今日撫有盈成而祖
宗之功德寧無可追述者乎誠以成湯受命固
以武德而開於先矣今襲湯號而爲武丁孫子
者秉乾德以爲治足以勝大任而有餘率乃祖
以攸行足以繼世德而無替故語其諸侯之助
祭也則建龍旗以于邁而十乘偕行奉大糦以
是將而群辟戾止人心之趨向何如也語其幅
隕之廣大也則千里邦畿固以列兆民之居處
而四海封域盡以屬一統之輿圖土宇之版章
punctuated:
同考試官教諭賈〔拱祿〕批：高宗中興，全在武德，作者多畧之。此篇得其肯綮，而氣象渾厚，不獨以文也錄之。
考試官教諭袁〔廷椿〕批：語莊而義密，商人頌德之意正如此。
考試官教諭楊〔舉〕批：典實。
詩人頌賢王繼統之休，以見世德之盛也。蓋武德以一天下，有商世濟其盛者也。然則所以承天休者，不亦至哉！此亦祭祀宗廟之樂也。蓋謂一代王業，不有所開，固無以啓永世之休；不有所繼，亦無以大光前之烈。今日撫有盈成，而祖宗之功德，寧無可追述者乎？誠以成湯受命，固以武德而開於先矣。今襲湯號而爲武丁孫子者，秉乾德以爲治，足以勝大任而有餘；率乃祖以攸行，足以繼世德而無替。故語其諸侯之助祭也，則建龍旗以于邁，而十乘偕行；奉大糦以是將，而群辟戾止。人心之趨向何如也！語其幅隕之廣大也，則千里邦畿，固以列兆民之居處；而四海封域，盡以屬一統之輿圖。土宇之版章
translation_en:
Comment by Associate Examiner and Instructor Jia Gonglu: “Gaozong’s restoration rested entirely on martial virtue, which writers commonly overlook. This essay grasps the essential point, and its manner is substantial and full. It is not solely for its literary merits that I select it.”
Comment by Examiner and Instructor Yuan Tingchun: “The language is dignified and the meaning closely reasoned. This is precisely the intent with which the people of Shang praised their ruler’s virtue.”
Comment by Examiner and Instructor Yang Ju: “Grounded in the classics and substantial.”
The poet praises the excellence of a worthy king’s succession to the throne, thereby displaying the abundance of virtue transmitted through the generations. It was through martial virtue that the realm was united, and the Shang dynasty sustained its flourishing from generation to generation. Was not its manner of receiving Heaven’s blessings therefore consummate? This, too, is music for sacrifices in the ancestral temple. Its meaning is that unless the royal enterprise of a dynasty has someone to found it, there can be no opening of blessings for endless generations; unless it has someone to carry it on, neither can the achievements of its predecessors be greatly glorified. Now that the king possesses a realm brought to fullness and completion, can there be no achievements and virtues of his ancestors worthy of recollection and narration?
Indeed, when Cheng Tang received the mandate, he established the foundation through martial virtue. Now Wu Ding, his descendant, who inherits Tang’s designation, governs by embodying the virtue of Qian, Heaven: he is more than equal to his great responsibilities. Following his ancestor in his conduct, he is fully able to perpetuate the virtue of his lineage without decline. Thus, to speak of the feudal lords’ assistance at the sacrifices: they raise dragon banners as they set forth, and ten chariots travel together; they reverently bear great offerings of sacrificial grain, and the assembled lords arrive. How the people’s hearts turn toward him! To speak of the vast extent of his territory [?]: within the royal domain of a thousand li are arrayed the dwellings of the myriad people, while all the lands within the Four Seas belong to the map of a unified realm. The registration and delineation of his territory [?]…

title: 嘉靖三十一年陝西鄉試錄
text:
何如也夫商邑四方之極也群后畢朝祁祁然
協恭以相祀視諸方命厥后者其一揆矣景山
殷命之始也大河旋列翼翼乎居中而制外視
諸奄有九有者其一致矣若此者固我武王乾
道之致抑孰非我商世德之貽者乎蓋正域四
方天之眷命於湯者宜矣而武丁克纘舊服視
於先而有光作民元后湯之受命於天者固矣
而武丁撫有成業質諸天而允合故世德所以
爲基命之原而萬福攸同即其人心歸附者可
===
徵也配命所以肇無疆之慶而繁祉大介即其
海宇清明者可知也然則今日得以享無窮之
利而致有廟之格者皆祖宗功德之所留爾升
歌之頃豈能忘其所自也耶雖然裕後以基命
者祖宗之澤也脩德以保業者守成之道也武
丁學於甘盤任於傅說其造就輔翊之功不淺
矣故能克紹先業而爲中興令主者良有以也
百世不遷之廟人心寧容已哉故當報本之時
稱宗德而本祖功推福澤而原帝命詩人之意
punctuated: 何如也？夫商邑，四方之極也。群后畢朝，祁祁然協恭以相祀，視諸方命厥后者，其一揆矣。景山，殷命之始也。大河旋列，翼翼乎居中而制外，視諸奄有九有者，其一致矣。若此者，固我武王乾道之致，抑孰非我商世德之貽者乎？蓋正域四方，天之眷命於湯者宜矣；而武丁克纘舊服，視於先而有光。作民元后，湯之受命於天者固矣；而武丁撫有成業，質諸天而允合。故世德所以爲基命之原，而萬福攸同，即其人心歸附者可徵也。配命所以肇無疆之慶，而繁祉大介，即其海宇清明者可知也。然則今日得以享無窮之利，而致有廟之格者，皆祖宗功德之所留爾。升歌之頃，豈能忘其所自也耶？雖然，裕後以基命者，祖宗之澤也；脩德以保業者，守成之道也。武丁學於甘盤，任於傅說，其造就輔翊之功不淺矣。故能克紹先業而爲中興令主者，良有以也。百世不遷之廟，人心寧容已哉？故當報本之時，稱宗德而本祖功，推福澤而原帝命。詩人之意
translation_en:
…how great was it? The capital of Shang was the pole toward which the four quarters turned. All the regional lords came to court; in their great numbers, they joined reverently in assisting at the sacrifices. Compared with the ordering of the lords throughout the regions, this followed the same principle. Mount Jing was where Yin’s mandate began. The great river wound about it, and, with reverent care, the ruler occupied the center and governed the lands beyond. Compared with possessing all the nine regions, this expressed the same purpose. Such achievements were indeed brought about by our martial king’s practice of the Way of Heaven; yet which of them was not also a legacy of our Shang dynasty’s virtue accumulated through the generations?

In setting right the territories of the four quarters, Tang fittingly received Heaven’s favor and mandate; and Wu Ding successfully continued the old charge, adding luster when measured against his predecessors. In becoming the people’s sovereign, Tang firmly received the mandate from Heaven; and Wu Ding maintained the established dominion, proving wholly in accord with Heaven when measured against it. Thus the virtue of successive generations was the source from which the mandate was founded, and all blessings converged upon him: the people’s willing allegiance provides evidence of this. His matching the mandate initiated boundless felicity, and abundant blessings greatly aided him: the peace and clarity throughout the realm make this apparent.

That today we may enjoy inexhaustible benefits and bring about the spirits’ arrival in the ancestral temple is entirely a legacy of our ancestors’ achievements and virtue. As the singers ascend to perform, how could we forget the source of these blessings? Nevertheless, enriching posterity and thereby laying the foundation of the mandate is the ancestors’ beneficence; cultivating virtue to preserve their achievement is the way to maintain an inherited order. Wu Ding studied under Gan Pan and entrusted responsibilities to Fu Yue. Their work in forming his character and assisting him was considerable. There was therefore good reason why he could continue his predecessors’ achievement and become an excellent ruler who restored the dynasty’s fortunes. How could people’s hearts allow the cessation of his worship in a temple whose tablet would remain unremoved for a hundred generations?

Thus, when repaying the source of their blessings, they praised the honored successor’s virtue while tracing it to the founding ancestor’s achievements; they traced the blessings and beneficence back to the mandate of the Lord on High. The poet’s intention…

title: 嘉靖三十一年陝西鄉試錄
text:
遠矣
春秋
夏公會鄭伯于時來　秋七月壬午公及
齊侯鄭伯入許〔俱隱公十有一年〕
寇靖
同考試官教諭周〔以魯〕批　〔士子類以鄭魯並看殊戾本〕
〔旨此篇融會傳意不缀不遺可以式矣錄之〕
考試官教諭袁〔廷椿〕批　〔親切簡嚴殆深於春秋者〕
考試官教諭楊〔舉〕批　〔意足詞暢諸作不及〕
===
春秋紀兵好辨內外之志而著內君之罪焉此
見時來會而許入雖鄭之志實魯有以成之也
春秋所以罪之者至矣且鄭莊要魯會講時來
巳而公及齊鄭連兵入許許君奔衛焉夫曰會
見圖許者鄭之志曰及見入許者魯之欲也是
鄭之罪不臧於魯而君子獨罪夫隱者何耶蓋
封建天下之公許太岳之裔先王之建國也莊
欲侵以自廣久矣想其好講時來必曰許鄰於
敝邑敝邑將有事焉請君率車賦以徼福於先
punctuated:
遠矣！

春秋
夏，公會鄭伯于時來。秋，七月壬午，公及齊侯、鄭伯入許。〔俱隱公十有一年〕
寇靖

同考試官教諭周〔以魯〕批：〔士子類以鄭魯並看，殊戾本〕〔旨。此篇融會傳意，不缀不遺，可以式矣，錄之。〕
考試官教諭袁〔廷椿〕批：〔親切簡嚴，殆深於春秋者。〕
考試官教諭楊〔舉〕批：〔意足詞暢，諸作不及。〕

春秋紀兵好，辨內外之志，而著內君之罪焉。此見時來會而許入，雖鄭之志，實魯有以成之也。春秋所以罪之者至矣。且鄭莊要魯，會講時來，巳而公及齊鄭連兵入許，許君奔衛焉。夫曰「會」，見圖許者鄭之志；曰「及」，見入許者魯之欲也。是鄭之罪不臧於魯，而君子獨罪夫隱者，何耶？蓋封建，天下之公；許，太岳之裔，先王之建國也。莊欲侵以自廣久矣。想其好講時來，必曰：「許鄰於敝邑，敝邑將有事焉。請君率車賦，以徼福於先
translation_en:
…far-reaching indeed!

Spring and Autumn Annals
“In summer, the Duke met the Earl of Zheng at Shilai. In autumn, in the seventh month, on the renwu day, the Duke, together with the Marquis of Qi and the Earl of Zheng, entered Xu.” 〔Both passages are from the eleventh year of Duke Yin.〕
Kou Jing

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhou Yilu, Instructor: 〔Candidates generally treat Zheng and Lu alike, seriously misconstruing the underlying〕〔meaning. This essay integrates the meaning of the commentaries, neither patching passages together nor omitting anything. It can serve as a model; include it.〕
Comment by Examiner Yuan Tingchun, Instructor: 〔Closely pertinent, concise, and rigorous: its author seems deeply versed in the Spring and Autumn Annals.〕
Comment by Examiner Yang Ju, Instructor: 〔The ideas are fully developed and the language flows freely; the other compositions do not match it.〕

In recording warfare and friendly relations, the Spring and Autumn Annals distinguishes the intentions of the home state and other states, and makes manifest the guilt of the home state's ruler. Here we see that, although the meeting at Shilai and the entry into Xu reflected Zheng's intentions, Lu in fact helped bring them to fruition. The Annals' condemnation is thus most emphatic. Duke Zhuang of Zheng invited Lu to meet and discuss friendly relations at Shilai. Subsequently, the Duke joined Qi and Zheng in combining their forces and entering Xu, and the ruler of Xu fled to Wei. The word “met” shows that plotting against Xu was Zheng's intention; the words “together with” show that entering Xu was Lu's desire. Zheng's wrongdoing was thus no less blameworthy than Lu's [?]. Why, then, does the gentleman particularly condemn Duke Yin?

The establishment of fiefs is a matter of public concern to all under Heaven. Xu, whose ruling house descended from Taiyue, was a state established by the former kings. Duke Zhuang had long wished to invade it and enlarge his own territory. We may imagine that, when he discussed friendly relations at Shilai, he must have said: “Xu borders our humble domain, and our humble domain intends to undertake military action there. I ask you, my lord, to lead your chariot levies, so as to seek blessings from the former…”

title: 嘉靖三十一年陝西鄉試錄
text:
君孤之願也爲隱計者盍辭曰列國疏封各有
分守凌弱犯寡王法不容則鄭莊雖雄焉攸逞
夫何感其利已遂其兼人許國是入也而民人
弗遑於啓處許君是逐也而鬼神弗享其禋祀
周麾一呼人見鄭師畢登也而不知揚其威者
魯實有以助之孫獲處西人知魯不與聞也而
不知歸於鄭者隱實欲以報之以許不入不足
以酬鄭之德曾何思保䘏寡小鄰之仁也徒厚
於鄭許何以堪耶以君不逐不足以剪鄭之忌
===
獨不思謹守王度臣之義也縱不䘏許獨不念
周耶覲禮廢而不脩變禮慢而不舉君子已謂
其無王以若所爲則惡極不可掩矣甲兵興以
擅土田取以專君子已議其不臣今又已甚其
罪大不可解矣昔周公夾輔之勳固不如是而
羽父篡氏之變其自貽之慼也故春秋時來書
會而入許稱及以見伐許者雖莊之志而成其
志者實隱之欲也其罪於是乎著矣雖然隱蓋
入於鄭莊術中而不知也大宫授兵莊之謀定
punctuated:
君，孤之願也。」爲隱計者，盍辭曰：「列國疏封，各有分守；凌弱犯寡，王法不容。」則鄭莊雖雄，焉攸逞？夫何感其利已，遂其兼人？許國是入也，而民人弗遑於啓處；許君是逐也，而鬼神弗享其禋祀。周麾一呼，人見鄭師畢登也，而不知揚其威者，魯實有以助之；孫獲處西，人知魯不與聞也，而不知歸於鄭者，隱實欲以報之。以許不入不足以酬鄭之德，曾何思保䘏寡小、鄰之仁也？徒厚於鄭，許何以堪耶？以君不逐不足以剪鄭之忌，獨不思謹守王度、臣之義也？縱不䘏許，獨不念周耶？
覲禮廢而不脩，變禮慢而不舉，君子已謂其無王；以若所爲，則惡極不可掩矣。甲兵興以擅，土田取以專，君子已議其不臣；今又已甚，其罪大不可解矣。昔周公夾輔之勳，固不如是，而羽父篡氏之變，其自貽之慼也。故《春秋》時來書「會」，而入許稱「及」，以見伐許者雖莊之志，而成其志者實隱之欲也。其罪於是乎著矣。
雖然，隱蓋入於鄭莊術中而不知也。大宫授兵，莊之謀定
translation_en:
…lord: this is my wish.” Why did those advising Duke Yin not decline, saying: “The various states were allotted their fiefs, and each has its own charge to maintain. To oppress the weak and attack those of little strength is intolerable under royal law”? Then, however formidable Duke Zhuang of Zheng might have been, where could he have given his ambitions free rein? Why, instead, was Duke Yin swayed by the advantage to himself into fulfilling the other’s desire to annex another state? The state of Xu was invaded, and its people had no respite, whether moving or resting; the ruler of Xu was expelled, and its spirits no longer received his pure sacrifices. At a single shout and a wave of the banner [?], people saw the troops of Zheng all scale the walls, but did not realize that Lu had in fact helped them display their might. When Sun Huo occupied the western part, people knew that Lu had taken no part in the deliberations, but did not realize that Duke Yin actually wished to repay Zheng by yielding the territory to it. He thought that nothing short of invading Xu would suffice to repay Zheng’s favor. When did he ever consider protecting and caring for the small and weak—the benevolence due from a neighbor? If he showed generosity only to Zheng, how could Xu endure it? He thought that nothing short of expelling Xu’s ruler would suffice to remove the object of Zheng’s apprehension. Did he never consider scrupulously observing royal standards—the duty of a subject? Even if he had no concern for Xu, did he have no regard for Zhou?
The rites of audience had fallen into disuse and were not restored; the rites for exceptional circumstances [?] were neglected and not performed. The gentleman already judged him to disregard the king. With conduct such as this, his wickedness reached an extreme that could no longer be concealed. He raised armies without authorization and seized lands on his own authority. The gentleman already censured him for failing in his duty as a subject. Now he went still further: his guilt was too great to excuse. The Duke of Zhou’s meritorious service in assisting the royal house was certainly not like this. The upheaval of Yufu’s usurpation [?] was a calamity Duke Yin brought upon himself. Thus, the Spring and Autumn Annals records “met” for Shilai, but uses “joined” for the invasion of Xu, showing that although attacking Xu was Duke Zhuang’s intention, bringing that intention to fruition was indeed Duke Yin’s desire. His guilt is thereby made manifest.
Nevertheless, Duke Yin had apparently fallen into Duke Zhuang of Zheng’s schemes without realizing it. When weapons were distributed at the grand ancestral temple, Duke Zhuang’s plan was settled…

title: 嘉靖三十一年陝西鄉試錄
text:
矣蝥弧先登莊之兵銳矣其會魯者懼掎角之
不成而魯擬其後也及其得許使許叔居許東
偏使公孫獲處許西偏許固鄭之內臣矣而又
外假存許之義內結許人之心莊真小人之雄
哉而左氏謂之知禮其失誣也夫
秦人伐晉〔文公三年〕吳子使札來聘〔襄公〕
〔二十有九年〕
朱櫂
同考試官教諭周〔以魯〕批〔發明聖人責備秦穆季札意〕
〔親切典雅其學春秋而深有得者乎錄之〕
考試官教諭袁〔廷譜〕批〔思致精深筆力清健〕
考試官教諭楊〔□〕批〔詞意莊重宜錄以式〕
===
觀春秋之責備有伐國以遂過者有讓國以階
亂者此秦穆封殽之役季子去吳之行春秋皆
責備焉其亦深惜之意與且于殽啓釁彭衙構
兵久矣秦穆之不忘於晉也今濟河焚舟將以
甘心亦當時報復之常也經於斯役而人之者
何蓋君子嘉復之不遠者苟有厭德既不足因
punctuated:
矣。蝥弧先登，莊之兵銳矣。其會魯者，懼掎角之不成，而魯擬其後也。及其得許，使許叔居許東偏，使公孫獲處許西偏，許固鄭之內臣矣。而又外假存許之義，內結許人之心，莊真小人之雄哉！而左氏謂之知禮，其失誣也夫！
秦人伐晉〔文公三年〕，吳子使札來聘〔襄公〕〔二十有九年〕。
朱櫂
同考試官教諭周〔以魯〕批〔發明聖人責備秦穆季札意，親切典雅，其學春秋而深有得者乎？錄之。〕
考試官教諭袁〔廷譜〕批〔思致精深，筆力清健。〕
考試官教諭楊〔□〕批〔詞意莊重，宜錄以式。〕
觀《春秋》之責備，有伐國以遂過者，有讓國以階亂者。此秦穆封殽之役、季子去吳之行，《春秋》皆責備焉，其亦深惜之意與！且于殽啓釁，彭衙構兵，久矣，秦穆之不忘於晉也。今濟河焚舟，將以甘心，亦當時報復之常也。經於斯役而人之者何？蓋君子嘉復之不遠者，苟有厭德，既不足因
translation_en:
…was already settled. With the Maohu banner the first to mount the walls, Duke Zhuang’s troops had shown their mettle. His reason for joining forces with Lu was his fear that a coordinated attack would fail and that Lu would threaten his rear. Once he had taken Xu, he had Xu Shu reside in its eastern part and Gongsun Huo occupy its western part: Xu was effectively already a subject of Zheng. Yet outwardly he borrowed the righteous pretext of preserving Xu, while inwardly winning over its people. Zhuang was truly a formidable figure among petty men! Yet Master Zuo called him knowledgeable in ritual propriety. How mistaken and misleading this was!
“The men of Qin attacked Jin” 〔Third year of Duke Wen〕; “The Viscount of Wu sent Zha on a diplomatic visit” 〔Duke Xiang〕〔Twenty-ninth year〕.
By Zhu Zhao 朱櫂.
Associate Examiner Zhou 〔Yilu〕, Instructor, comments: 〔He elucidates the Sage’s intention in demanding exemplary conduct of Duke Mu of Qin and Ji Zha. His treatment is pertinent and classically elegant. Surely he has studied the Spring and Autumn Annals and attained a profound understanding of it? Include this essay.〕
Examiner Yuan 〔Tingpu〕, Instructor, comments: 〔The conception is refined and profound; the writing lucid and vigorous.〕
Examiner Yang 〔□〕, Instructor, comments: 〔The language and ideas are dignified. It should be included as a model.〕
Considering how the Spring and Autumn Annals demands exemplary conduct, we find those who attack another state and thereby persist in their faults, and those who yield a state and thereby open the way to disorder. Such were Duke Mu of Qin’s expedition at Yao [?] and Master Ji’s departure from Wu. The Spring and Autumn Annals demands exemplary conduct of both: does this not also express profound regret for them?
Hostilities began at Yao, and fighting ensued at Pengya: Duke Mu of Qin had long been unable to put Jin out of his mind. Now he crossed the Yellow River and burned his boats, intending to satisfy his resentment. This, too, was ordinary retaliatory conduct for that age. Why, then, does the Classic refer to him in this campaign merely as one of the “men” of Qin? The gentleman commends those who return to the right path before straying far. If someone possesses odious moral qualities, he does not even afford grounds through which to…

title: 嘉靖三十一年陝西鄉試錄
text:
之以著義又不足藉之以示懲聖人何責焉唯
穆也于殽潰北之後作誓自新所貴者良士惄
惻周邦家之慮所思者彥聖諄復重治理之圖
將來之善蓋可冀矣何意其復有是舉耶易言
有不善未嘗不知知之未嘗復行所以重顏氏
之子者惟其不二過耳穆蓋未之能也故必待
新城之圍方悔前事之誤噫何其晚乎是故書
人所以責秦穆者以此謁示世及光請歸正甚
矣季子之不屑有吳也乃去之延陵將以削迹
===
固一時志節之優也經於來聘而名之者何蓋
君子達節而不守者苟執小諒大之不足以康
國家次之不足以奠宗冑聖人奚取焉若札也
夷昧既終之後幡然改圖語其序既協人紀之
常論其賢尤堪社稷之托光僚之變斯可弭者
抑何意其執而不變耶書載唐虞傳賢而三代
傳子所以高帝王之義者惟其不有已耳札固
莫之省也是以致容室之甲成叛亂之禍噫誰
所貽乎是故書名所以責季札者以此吁知責
punctuated:
之以著義，又不足藉之以示懲，聖人何責焉？唯穆也，于殽潰北之後，作誓自新，所貴者良士，惄惻周邦家之慮；所思者彥聖，諄復重治理之圖。將來之善，蓋可冀矣，何意其復有是舉耶？易言：「有不善未嘗不知，知之未嘗復行。」所以重顏氏之子者，惟其不二過耳。穆蓋未之能也，故必待新城之圍，方悔前事之誤。噫，何其晚乎！是故書人所以責秦穆者，以此。
謁示世及，光請歸正，甚矣季子之不屑有吳也！乃去之延陵，將以削迹，固一時志節之優也。經於來聘而名之者何？蓋君子達節而不守者，苟執小諒，大之不足以康國家，次之不足以奠宗冑，聖人奚取焉？若札也，夷昧既終之後，幡然改圖，語其序，既協人紀之常；論其賢，尤堪社稷之托。光僚之變，斯可弭者，抑何意其執而不變耶？書載唐虞傳賢，而三代傳子，所以高帝王之義者，惟其不有已耳。札固莫之省也，是以致容室之甲，成叛亂之禍。噫，誰所貽乎！是故書名所以責季札者，以此。吁，知責
translation_en:
…him to make righteousness manifest, nor is he fit to serve as an example of admonition: what would the Sage have to reproach him for? But Mu, after his defeat and rout at Yao, composed an oath to reform himself. He prized worthy men, his sorrowful concern encompassing the whole state; he longed for accomplished and sagely men, earnestly reiterating his plans for good government. Surely one could hope for goodness from him thereafter. Who would have expected him to undertake such an action again? The Book of Changes says: “Whenever he did anything wrong, he invariably knew it; once he knew it, he never did it again.” The reason it esteems the son of the Yan family is simply that he never repeated a fault. Mu evidently could not achieve this. Thus it was only at the siege of Xincheng that he regretted his earlier mistakes. Alas, how late it was! This, then, is why recording him as a mere “man” serves to censure Duke Mu of Qin.
Yan proclaimed succession from brother to brother, and Guang requested that the throne be restored to its rightful holder [?]. How profoundly Jizi disdained possession of Wu! He withdrew to Yanling, intending to efface his traces. Certainly, his resolve and integrity were outstanding in his day. Why, then, does the Classic record him by personal name when he came on a diplomatic visit? The gentleman understands how to adapt his principles rather than adhering rigidly to them. If someone clings to a petty fidelity that cannot, at best, bring peace to the state, or even, at a lesser level, secure the ruling lineage, what would the Sage find commendable in him? Had Zha decisively changed his plans after Yimei’s death, his place in the succession would have accorded with the regular order of human relationships; and his worthiness would have made him especially fit to be entrusted with the altars of soil and grain. The upheaval involving Guang and Liao could thereby have been averted. Who would have expected him to persist without changing? The Book of Documents records that Tang and Yu transmitted rule to worthy men, whereas the Three Dynasties transmitted it to sons. The reason it exalts the righteousness of these emperors and kings is simply that they were free of selfishness. Zha, however, failed to reflect on this. Consequently, he brought about the armed men in the chamber [?] and the calamity of rebellion. Alas, who brought this upon them? This, then, is why recording Ji Zha by personal name serves to censure him. Ah, to understand the censure…

title: 嘉靖三十一年陝西鄉試錄
text:
穆則貳過者有所警而不憚于改知責札則孰
一者有所懲而自處以中聖人致望之意微矣
雖然刪書而序秦誓過吳而弔季子夫子于穆
與札待之甚恕又如此于以見聖人之心可以
訓後世則取善不遺可以勵風節札固未嘗深
論也不然以人廢言病守身而貧亂臣之口將
不紛紛矣乎
禮記
故人者天地之心也五行之端也
趙守憲
同考試官教諭王〔寔賓〕批〔心端二字以理氣言此篇體認〕
〔精切蓋究心於造化者〕
考試官教諭袁〔廷椿〕批〔純正〕
考試官教諭楊〔舉〕批〔詞理雅健〕
記者原人之有生具造化理氣之全焉夫人不
能外造化以有生也而皆具理氣之全焉可不
知所以自盡乎宜記者推原其故以示人也想
其意曰人之有生也固爲天地之貴而實具造
punctuated:
穆，則貳過者有所警而不憚于改；知責札，則孰一者有所懲而自處以中。聖人致望之意微矣！雖然，刪書而序秦誓，過吳而弔季子，夫子于穆與札，待之甚恕又如此。于以見聖人之心，可以訓後世，則取善不遺；可以勵風節，札固未嘗深論也。不然，以人廢言，病守身而貧亂臣之口，將不紛紛矣乎？
禮記
故人者，天地之心也，五行之端也。
趙守憲
同考試官教諭王〔寔賓〕批：〔心端二字以理氣言，此篇體認〕〔精切，蓋究心於造化者。〕
考試官教諭袁〔廷椿〕批：〔純正。〕
考試官教諭楊〔舉〕批：〔詞理雅健。〕
記者原人之有生，具造化理氣之全焉。夫人不能外造化以有生也，而皆具理氣之全焉，可不知所以自盡乎？宜記者推原其故以示人也。想其意曰：人之有生也，固爲天地之貴，而實具造
translation_en:
…Mu, then those who repeat their errors will take warning and not shrink from reform; understanding the censure of Zha, those who cling rigidly to a single course [?] will take heed and conduct themselves according to the mean. Subtle indeed is the sage’s intention in expressing his hopes for them! Nevertheless, in editing the Documents he placed the Oath of Qin in its sequence, and on passing through Wu he paid his respects to Jizi. Such was the Master’s generous treatment of Mu and Zha. Here we can see the sage’s heart: whatever could instruct later generations, he preserved, overlooking nothing good; where conduct could encourage moral integrity, he did not subject Zha to searching criticism. Otherwise, if one rejected words because of the speaker and condemned the preservation of personal integrity, thereby giving rebellious ministers something to say [?], would their arguments not proliferate?

Record of Rites
“Thus the human being is the heart of Heaven and Earth and the culmination of the Five Phases.”

Zhao Shouxian

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang Shibin, Instructor: “The two words ‘heart’ and ‘culmination’ are discussed in terms of principle and material force. This essay’s understanding is precise and incisive; its author has evidently devoted thought to the processes of creation and transformation.”

Comment by Examiner Yuan Tingchun, Instructor: “Pure and orthodox.”

Comment by Examiner Yang Ju, Instructor: “Elegant and vigorous in both expression and reasoning.”

The author of the Record traces human life to its source: human beings possess the full complement of principle and material force involved in creation and transformation. Human beings cannot come into existence apart from these processes, and all possess principle and material force in their entirety. Can they then fail to understand how to realize their own capacities fully? It is fitting that the author of the Record should trace the reason for this to its source and reveal it to others. We may imagine his meaning as follows: human beings, in coming into existence, are indeed the most honored beings between Heaven and Earth, and truly possess the entirety of creation…

title: 嘉靖三十一年陝西鄉試錄
text:
化之全然造化之具于人者理氣而已矣何也
天地無心而成化人亦奚爲而心天地之心耶
蓋天地主宰而其心淵焉夫物咸受之也惟人
則有以會其精而虛靈之具一淸寧之本也明
覺之眞一易簡之良也曰仁與禮誠之通也反
之吾心而自足曰義與智誠之復也求之吾性
而有餘卽夫一心之感通寔爲兩儀之秘藏也
天地無心而人爲之心矣無心之心其諸異象
而同體者乎五行循環而無端人亦奚爲而求
===
端于五行耶蓋五氣順布而其端大焉夫物咸
受之也惟人則有以得其全動靜之爲根一屈
伸之相感也剛柔之異質一變化之無窮也曰
視曰聽而得于妙合之凝者有以顯諸仁曰貌
曰言曰思而本于絪緼之感者有以藏諸用卽
夫一身之運動寔爲五氣之流行也五行無端
而人爲之端矣無端之端其諸異形而同用者
乎由是觀之則天地之塞吾其體天地之帥吾
其性君子可不踐形盡性以自充耶雖然此章
punctuated: 化之全。然造化之具于人者，理氣而已矣。何也？天地無心而成化，人亦奚爲而心天地之心耶？蓋天地主宰，而其心淵焉。夫物咸受之也，惟人則有以會其精，而虛靈之具，一淸寧之本也；明覺之眞，一易簡之良也。曰仁與禮，誠之通也，反之吾心而自足；曰義與智，誠之復也，求之吾性而有餘。卽夫一心之感通，寔爲兩儀之秘藏也。天地無心，而人爲之心矣。無心之心，其諸異象而同體者乎？五行循環而無端，人亦奚爲而求端于五行耶？蓋五氣順布，而其端大焉。夫物咸受之也，惟人則有以得其全。動靜之爲根，一屈伸之相感也；剛柔之異質，一變化之無窮也。曰視曰聽，而得于妙合之凝者，有以顯諸仁；曰貌曰言曰思，而本于絪緼之感者，有以藏諸用。卽夫一身之運動，寔爲五氣之流行也。五行無端，而人爲之端矣。無端之端，其諸異形而同用者乎？由是觀之，則天地之塞，吾其體；天地之帥，吾其性。君子可不踐形盡性以自充耶？雖然，此章
translation_en: …the fullness of creation and transformation. Yet what human beings possess of creation and transformation is simply principle and material force (qi). Why is this? Heaven and Earth accomplish their transformations without a mind; how, then, do human beings make the mind of Heaven and Earth their own? Heaven and Earth govern all things, and their mind is profound. All things receive it, but human beings alone can gather its finest essence. Their capacity for empty, numinous awareness is one with the foundation of Heaven’s clarity and Earth’s tranquility; the genuineness of their lucid awareness is one with the excellence of ease and simplicity. Benevolence and ritual propriety are the outward communication of sincerity: turning back to seek them in our minds, we find ourselves fully supplied. Righteousness and wisdom are the return of sincerity: seeking them in our nature, we find more than enough. The responsive communion of a single mind is indeed the hidden treasury of the two cosmic powers, Heaven and Earth. Heaven and Earth have no mind, yet human beings serve as their mind. Is this mind of what has no mind not different in manifestation yet identical in substance? The Five Phases revolve without a beginning; how, then, do human beings seek a beginning in the Five Phases? The five material forces spread in due order, and their beginnings are vast. All things receive them, but human beings alone can obtain their fullness. Movement and stillness serving as roots are one with the mutual responsiveness of contraction and expansion; the differing constitutions of hardness and softness are one with the inexhaustibility of change and transformation. Sight and hearing, obtained through the condensation of a wondrous union, provide the means for manifestation in benevolence; demeanor, speech, and thought, rooted in the interaction of intertwined cosmic forces, provide the means for concealment within functioning. The movements of a single body are indeed the circulation of the five material forces. The Five Phases have no beginning, yet human beings serve as their beginning. Is this beginning of what has no beginning not different in form yet identical in function? Viewed in this way, that which fills Heaven and Earth constitutes my body; that which commands Heaven and Earth constitutes my nature. Can the gentleman fail to fulfill his bodily form and fully realize his nature, thereby bringing himself to completion? Nevertheless, this chapter…

title: 嘉靖三十一年陝西鄉試錄
text:
論禮而發蓋必如是而禮之本立禮之用行矣
故古之聖人建極以爲天下正合德天地合明
日月合序四時而後操制作之權以明禮蓋無
不當者然其源不外理氣克全而已矣善乎程
子之言曰論性不論氣不備論氣不論性不明
知此說者其達大禮之本乎
樂者心之動也聲者樂之象也文采節奏
聲之飾也君子動其本樂其象然後治
其飾
邢子深
===
同考試官教諭王〔室賓〕批〔由本及文之意此作發明精〕
透是學樂而有得者可錄
考試官教諭袁〔廷儁〕批〔格律詞雅〕
考試官教諭楊〔舉〕批〔簡重〕
記者論樂有本而有文君子之作因之焉甚矣
本文兼備樂之所以全也而君子之作其能外
是哉今夫樂之爲道也固非出于僞爲而君子
之于樂也亦不容以强作夫樂何爲而生也心
punctuated:
論禮而發，蓋必如是而禮之本立，禮之用行矣。故古之聖人建極以爲天下正，合德天地，合明日月，合序四時，而後操制作之權以明禮，蓋無不當者。然其源不外理氣克全而已矣。善乎程子之言曰：「論性不論氣，不備；論氣不論性，不明。」知此說者，其達大禮之本乎？

樂者，心之動也；聲者，樂之象也；文采節奏，聲之飾也。君子動其本，樂其象，然後治其飾。
邢子深

同考試官教諭王〔室賓〕批〔由本及文之意，此作發明精〕透，是學樂而有得者，可錄。
考試官教諭袁〔廷儁〕批〔格律詞雅〕
考試官教諭楊〔舉〕批〔簡重〕

記者論樂有本而有文，君子之作因之焉。甚矣，本文兼備，樂之所以全也，而君子之作，其能外是哉？今夫樂之爲道也，固非出于僞爲，而君子之于樂也，亦不容以强作。夫樂何爲而生也？心
translation_en:
…arises from a discussion of ritual. Only in this way can the foundation of ritual be established and its functions put into practice. Thus the sages of antiquity established the supreme standard to set the world aright, matching their virtue with Heaven and Earth, their brightness with the sun and moon, and their ordering with the four seasons. Only then did they exercise the authority to create institutions and clarify ritual, so that nothing was inappropriate. Yet the source of this lay simply in fully realizing principle and material force. How well Master Cheng put it: “To discuss nature without discussing material force is incomplete; to discuss material force without discussing nature is unclear.” Would not someone who understands this teaching comprehend the foundation of the great rites?

“Music is the movement of the heart; sound is the manifestation of music; patterned embellishment and rhythm are the adornment of sound. The gentleman stirs its foundation, delights in its manifestation, and only then attends to its adornment.”
Xing Zishen

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang Shibin, Instructor: “This composition explains with precision and thoroughness the idea of proceeding from the foundation to its patterned expression. Its author has studied music and gained understanding. It merits inclusion.”
Comment by Examiner Yuan Tingjun, Instructor: “The form and diction are elegant [?].”
Comment by Examiner Yang Ju, Instructor: “Concise and weighty.”

The recorder discusses music as possessing both a foundation and patterned expression; the gentleman follows these in creating it. How essential it is that foundation and patterned expression both be present: this is what makes music complete. Could the gentleman’s creation of music lie outside this principle? Now, the Way of music certainly does not arise from contrivance, and the gentleman, in his approach to music, likewise cannot force its creation. How, then, does music arise? The heart…

title: 嘉靖三十一年陝西鄉試錄
text:
之動也蓋性貞旣感雖因物以有遷而平中所
由亦順應而不射根于靜者發于動者也斯樂
之所以始乎夫聲何爲而作也樂之象也蓋辭
意相應而一元有以導其機和順允宣而五音
有以兆其節得之寂者妙之感者也斯樂之所
由顯乎以至德盛而文采以明情深而節奏自
著動乎容也成文而可觀播乎器也從律而不
亂而樂之飾也其盛矣乎是以君子之作樂也
知樂有本矣于是反情以適志審一以定和而
===
吾心爲之順動焉知樂有聲矣于是乎淸濁之
宣適高下之變而大音莫之沾懘焉由是不但
已也治其容以飾其威而干戚羽旄之用備治
其聲以飾其喜而琴瑟管籥之象昭著于有節
者始于無形者以本之也發于極文者根于至
質者以先之也而作樂之序斯其不紊乎由此
言之無心固不足以爲樂而無物亦不足以爲
全先王之樂可謂盛矣而君子之作也豈苟焉
而已哉抑此章本文內外之樂卽道器之說也
punctuated: 之動也。蓋性貞旣感，雖因物以有遷，而平中所由，亦順應而不射。根于靜者，發于動者也，斯樂之所以始乎！夫聲何爲而作也？樂之象也。蓋辭意相應，而一元有以導其機；和順允宣，而五音有以兆其節。得之寂者，妙之感者也，斯樂之所由顯乎！以至德盛而文采以明，情深而節奏自著。動乎容也，成文而可觀；播乎器也，從律而不亂。而樂之飾也，其盛矣乎！是以君子之作樂也，知樂有本矣，于是反情以適志，審一以定和，而吾心爲之順動焉。知樂有聲矣，于是乎淸濁之宣，適高下之變，而大音莫之沾懘焉。由是不但已也，治其容以飾其威，而干戚羽旄之用備；治其聲以飾其喜，而琴瑟管籥之象昭。著于有節者，始于無形者以本之也；發于極文者，根于至質者以先之也。而作樂之序，斯其不紊乎！由此言之，無心固不足以爲樂，而無物亦不足以爲全。先王之樂可謂盛矣，而君子之作也，豈苟焉而已哉！抑此章本文內外之樂，卽道器之說也。
translation_en:
…the movement of the heart. For when the steadfast nature is affected [?], although it changes in response to external things, the source of its balance and centrality likewise responds compliantly without deviation [?]. What is rooted in stillness emerges in movement: is this not how music begins? Why does sound arise? It is the manifestation of music. Words and intentions correspond, and the single primal source guides their incipient movement; harmony and compliance find full expression, and the five tones give the first indications of their rhythmic divisions. What is apprehended in stillness finds its subtle realization in response to stimuli: is this not how music becomes manifest? Thus, when virtue flourishes, its patterned beauty shines forth; when feeling is deep, rhythm becomes evident of itself. Expressed in bodily movement, it forms patterns worthy of contemplation; sounded through instruments, it follows the pitch standards without disorder. How splendid are the embellishments of music!

Thus, when the gentleman makes music, he knows that music has a foundation. He therefore returns to his feelings to bring his intentions into accord, and examines unity to establish harmony; his heart consequently moves in compliance. Knowing that music has sound, he gives expression to clear and deep tones and accommodates changes of high and low, so that the great sound suffers no discord. Nor does he stop there. He orders bodily movements to embellish their dignity, fully providing for the use of shields, battle-axes, feathers, and yak-tail standards; he orders sounds to embellish joy, making manifest the musical forms of zithers, pipes, and flutes. What becomes evident in measured rhythm begins in the formless, which supplies its foundation; what emerges in the utmost elaboration is rooted in the utmost simplicity, which takes precedence. Is not the sequence of making music thereby kept in order?

Viewed in this light, without the heart there can certainly be no music, yet without material things music cannot attain completeness either. The music of the former kings may indeed be called magnificent. Could the gentleman’s making of music, then, be merely a casual undertaking? Moreover, this chapter’s account of music in its foundation and embellishment, its inward and outward aspects, is precisely an account of the Way and concrete instruments.

title: 嘉靖三十一年陝西鄉試錄
text:
蓋道形而上者器形而下者可相有而不可相
無嬰之先後之序不容紊耳柰世之作樂者徒
事其文而不求其本此季子所以有感于韶而
乙也曠也涓也之告其君者恒切切也噫當時
悟而究其本焉樂其可興乎
第貳場
論
士不可以不弘毅
周鑑
同考試官教諭賈〔拱辰〕批　詞理精明氣象宏遠眞得曾子
考試官教諭袁〔廷椿〕批　雄渾精深
考試官教諭楊〔謇〕批　氣昌辭偉
心法錄之
論曰君子之道極於其盡性故不容不大其心
以體之性出於天而具於人心統乎性以合乎
天天其宰也性其命也心其包廓而運用也故
天至大性亦至大性至大心亦至大其理一其
道同也故君子不大其心不可以言性不盡其
punctuated:
蓋道，形而上者；器，形而下者。可相有而不可相無，嬰之先後之序不容紊耳。柰世之作樂者，徒事其文而不求其本，此季子所以有感于韶，而乙也、曠也、涓也之告其君者恒切切也。噫！當時悟而究其本焉，樂其可興乎？

第貳場
論
士不可以不弘毅
周鑑

同考試官教諭賈〔拱辰〕批：詞理精明，氣象宏遠，眞得曾子
考試官教諭袁〔廷椿〕批：雄渾精深。
考試官教諭楊〔謇〕批：氣昌辭偉。
心法，錄之。

論曰：君子之道極於其盡性，故不容不大其心以體之。性出於天而具於人，心統乎性以合乎天。天，其宰也；性，其命也；心，其包廓而運用也。故天至大，性亦至大；性至大，心亦至大。其理一，其道同也。故君子不大其心，不可以言性；不盡其
translation_en:
For the Way is what lies above physical form; implements are what lie below physical form. They can coexist, but neither can exist without the other. Their order of precedence must not be confused [?]. Yet those who make music in this world merely attend to its embellishments without seeking its foundation. This is why Jizi was moved by the Shao music, and why Yi, Kuang, and Juan were always so earnest in their admonitions to their rulers. Alas! If those of the time awakened to this and investigated its foundation, might music flourish again?

Second Session
Discourse
“A Scholar Must Be Broad-minded and Resolute”
Zhou Jian

Comment by Associate Examiner Jia Gongchen, Instructor: “The language and reasoning are lucid and precise; the spirit is expansive and far-reaching. It truly grasps Zengzi’s teaching of the mind. Include it.” [The last words of this comment appear below the other two comments in the transcription.]
Comment by Examiner Yuan Tingchun, Instructor: “Powerful and full-bodied, refined and profound.”
Comment by Examiner Yang Jian, Instructor: “Abundant vitality and magnificent diction.”

Thus Heaven is supremely great, and human nature is likewise supremely great; human nature is supremely great, and the mind is likewise supremely great. title: 嘉靖三十一年陝西鄉試錄
text:
性不可以言天不可以言道是故言
天下之弘而不可量也言天下之毅而不可抑
也而後可以言心之大言天下之重而不可載
也言天下之遠而不可極也而後可以言性之
大心以體性性以達天斯其至矣夫天則不可
測也以求諸性性則不可窮也以求諸心故君
子之道一惟審其端而已矣曾子曰士不可以
不弘毅意蓋如此夫天生人而賦之性豈偶然
哉固將使之盡焉以行其道所謂盡己之性以
===
盡人之性盡人之性以盡物之性者也所謂賛
天地之化育以與天地參者也夫物芸然萬矣
夫人夥然億兆矣夫化育灝然廣矣夫天地嘳
然確然神矣而予玆藐然混乎其中則亦物而
已矣而盡之賛之參之何爲而屬之吾亦何爲
而遂盡遂賛遂參而無歉哉此天下百慮而一
致萬象異形而同體者也故觀物於百萬則不
容以不殊觀性於一同則統有宗而會有元而
舉世無餘蘊焉性之所以爲大也易稱乾元資
punctuated: 性，不可以言天，不可以言道。是故，言天下之弘而不可量也，言天下之毅而不可抑也，而後可以言心之大；言天下之重而不可載也，言天下之遠而不可極也，而後可以言性之大。心以體性，性以達天，斯其至矣。夫天則不可測也，以求諸性；性則不可窮也，以求諸心。故君子之道，一惟審其端而已矣。曾子曰：「士不可以不弘毅。」意蓋如此。夫天生人而賦之性，豈偶然哉？固將使之盡焉，以行其道。所謂盡己之性以盡人之性，盡人之性以盡物之性者也；所謂賛天地之化育，以與天地參者也。夫物芸然萬矣，夫人夥然億兆矣，夫化育灝然廣矣，夫天地嘳然確然神矣。而予玆藐然混乎其中，則亦物而已矣。而盡之、賛之、參之，何爲而屬之吾？亦何爲而遂盡、遂賛、遂參而無歉哉？此天下百慮而一致，萬象異形而同體者也。故觀物於百萬，則不容以不殊；觀性於一同，則統有宗而會有元，而舉世無餘蘊焉。性之所以爲大也。《易》稱：「乾元資
translation_en:
…one’s nature, one cannot speak of Heaven, nor can one speak of the Way. Thus, only after speaking of a breadth throughout the world that cannot be measured, and a resolve throughout the world that cannot be checked, can one speak of the greatness of the mind. Only after speaking of a weight throughout the world that cannot be borne, and a distance throughout the world whose end cannot be reached, can one speak of the greatness of human nature. Through the mind one embodies one’s nature; through one’s nature one reaches Heaven. This is the ultimate attainment. Heaven cannot be fathomed, so one seeks it in one’s nature; one’s nature cannot be exhausted, so one seeks it in the mind. Thus the way of the gentleman consists solely in discerning its beginnings. Zengzi said, “A scholar must be broad-minded and resolute.” His meaning was surely this. Could Heaven’s giving birth to human beings and endowing them with their nature be accidental? Surely its purpose was that they should fully realize that nature and thereby practice its Way. This is what is meant by fully realizing one’s own nature so as to fully realize the nature of others, and fully realizing the nature of others so as to fully realize the nature of things. It is what is meant by assisting the transforming and nourishing powers of Heaven and Earth, and thereby forming a triad with them.

Things flourish in their myriads; human beings throng in their countless millions; transformation and nourishment extend with boundless vastness; Heaven and Earth are [?], firm, and wondrous. Yet I, so insignificant, mingling among them, am merely another thing. Why, then, is it assigned to me to fully realize these natures, assist these powers, and stand alongside Heaven and Earth? And how can I accomplish this realization, assistance, and participation without falling short? It is because the world’s hundred deliberations converge upon one end, and its myriad manifestations, though different in form, share one substance. Thus, when we view things in their millions, they cannot but be distinct; when we view their nature in its unity, their integration has a governing source and their convergence has an origin, leaving nothing hidden throughout the world. This is why nature is great. The Book of Changes says, “Qian’s primal power, upon which …

title: 嘉靖三十一年陝西鄉試錄
text:
始雲行雨施品物流形乃統天元者善之長也
君子體仁足以長人又曰天地之大德曰生聖
人之大寶曰位何以守位曰仁其言性之德乎
故天德莫大乎仁人道莫大乎體仁天無私故
廣運而不息不冒而無外聖人無欲故任重而
不傾道遠而無蹶其寂冲漠無朕而無所不具
其感大通而無所不達故情有喜怒哀樂愛惡
則達之以和性有易直子諒恭敬辨別則制之
以中禮有制度文章車輿衣服宮室飲食吉凶
===
軍賓之文則本之以質樂有鍾鼓磬管琴瑟羽
旄聲音律呂之變則合之以節刑有賞慶征伐
政有紀綱名物之序則陳之以彝物有山林川
澤原隰鳥獸草木昆蟲之化則裁之以宜民有
田廬樹畜術黨學習老幼媰卹之生則育之以
順天地有施有養有寒暑災祥之異覆載生成
之殊則通之裁成而匡之輔相蓋自天地人物
以反之吾身由吾身以極乎天下咸一體也咸
一體則咸一心也咸一心則咸一仁也天地以
punctuated: 始，雲行雨施，品物流形，乃統天。元者，善之長也；君子體仁，足以長人。又曰：「天地之大德曰生，聖人之大寶曰位。何以守位？曰仁。」其言性之德乎！故天德莫大乎仁，人道莫大乎體仁。天無私，故廣運而不息，不冒而無外；聖人無欲，故任重而不傾，道遠而無蹶。其寂，冲漠無朕而無所不具；其感，大通而無所不達。故情有喜怒哀樂愛惡，則達之以和；性有易直子諒恭敬辨別，則制之以中；禮有制度文章、車輿衣服、宮室飲食、吉凶軍賓之文，則本之以質；樂有鍾鼓磬管、琴瑟羽旄、聲音律呂之變，則合之以節；刑有賞慶征伐，政有紀綱名物之序，則陳之以彝；物有山林川澤、原隰鳥獸、草木昆蟲之化，則裁之以宜；民有田廬樹畜、術黨學習、老幼媰卹之生，則育之以順；天地有施有養，有寒暑災祥之異、覆載生成之殊，則通之裁成，而匡之輔相。蓋自天地人物以反之吾身，由吾身以極乎天下，咸一體也。咸一體則咸一心也，咸一心則咸一仁也。天地以
translation_en:
…their beginning; clouds move and rain falls, and the myriad things flow into their forms: thus it encompasses Heaven. The originating power is the foremost of goodness; the gentleman embodies benevolence and is thereby able to lead others. It also says: “The great virtue of Heaven and Earth is called life; the great treasure of the sage is called position. By what does he maintain his position? Benevolence.” Is this not speaking of the virtue of human nature? Thus no virtue of Heaven is greater than benevolence, and nothing in the human Way is greater than embodying benevolence. Heaven has no partiality; hence its vast workings never cease, and it does not encroach [?], yet nothing lies outside it. The sage has no selfish desires; hence he bears a heavy responsibility without toppling and travels a distant way without stumbling. In stillness, he is empty and silent, without any perceptible trace, yet contains everything; in responding, he comprehends all and reaches everywhere.

Thus, where the feelings comprise joy, anger, sorrow, pleasure, love, and hatred, he brings them to expression through harmony. Where human nature comprises mildness, uprightness, kindness and trustworthiness [?], reverence, and discrimination, he regulates them through the mean. Where ritual comprises institutions and patterned forms, carriages and clothing, dwellings and food, and the observances for auspicious occasions, mourning, military affairs, and guests, he roots them in substance. Where music comprises the variations of bells, drums, chime stones, pipes, zithers, feather and yak-tail banners, sounds, and pitch standards, he brings them into accord through measured rhythm. Where penal authority comprises rewards, commendations, punitive expeditions, and attacks, and government comprises the ordering of guiding principles, names, and things, he sets them forth according to constant norms. Where the world of things comprises the transformations of mountains, forests, rivers, marshes, uplands, lowlands, birds, beasts, plants, and insects, he regulates them according to what is fitting. Where the people's livelihood comprises fields and dwellings, planting and animal husbandry, local communities [?] and learning, and provision for the old, the young, pregnant women, and those needing relief [?], he nurtures it by following its proper course. Where Heaven and Earth bestow and nourish, with the alternations of cold and heat, calamities and auspicious signs, and their distinct functions of covering and supporting, generating and completing, he comprehends these workings and gives them due form, rectifying and assisting them.

From Heaven and Earth, people and things, one turns back to one's own person; from one's own person, one reaches throughout all under Heaven: all form one body. If all form one body, all share one mind; if all share one mind, all share one benevolence. Heaven and Earth, through…

title: 嘉靖三十一年陝西鄉試錄
text:
仁普萬物而爲心聖人以心體萬物而爲仁故
天下之繫乎我者若是其重也而任之若是其
遠也而道之然任之不可以力勝道之不可以
步致則亦本之吾心以體之以寛廣則謂之弘
焉以强忍則謂之毅焉而何與於仁乎仁即心
也其本然則至靜而無欲者也無欲則寛裕溫
柔足以有容發强剛毅足以有執而所謂重且
遠者於是乎出焉非此心之外別有一仁也非
仁之外別有一弘毅也非弘毅之外別有一重
===
遠也惟人心本大而形氣梏之故形生而役之
者衆矣知發而誘之者繁矣以衆繁之欲塞虛
靈之舍幾何而不小哉故其弘誠大矣貪競鄙
詐用知自私之念入焉而隘其毅誠大矣回利
怵威頽靡怠惰之習入焉而萎其重且遠者誠
大矣褊陋廢墜之敝入焉而阻故君子省察所
以審微克治所以敦復存誠所以祛妄主敬所
以立誠隘者以去而吾之弘自如也萎者以去
而吾之毅自如也阻者以去而吾之重且遠者
punctuated:
仁普萬物而爲心，聖人以心體萬物而爲仁。故天下之繫乎我者，若是其重也，而任之；若是其遠也，而道之。然任之不可以力勝，道之不可以步致，則亦本之吾心以體之。以寛廣則謂之弘焉，以强忍則謂之毅焉，而何與於仁乎？仁即心也，其本然則至靜而無欲者也。無欲則寛裕溫柔足以有容，發强剛毅足以有執，而所謂重且遠者於是乎出焉。非此心之外別有一仁也，非仁之外別有一弘毅也，非弘毅之外別有一重遠也。
惟人心本大，而形氣梏之，故形生而役之者衆矣，知發而誘之者繁矣。以衆繁之欲塞虛靈之舍，幾何而不小哉？故其弘誠大矣，貪競鄙詐、用知自私之念入焉而隘；其毅誠大矣，回利怵威、頽靡怠惰之習入焉而萎；其重且遠者誠大矣，褊陋廢墜之敝入焉而阻。故君子省察所以審微，克治所以敦復，存誠所以祛妄，主敬所以立誠。隘者以去，而吾之弘自如也；萎者以去，而吾之毅自如也；阻者以去，而吾之重且遠者
translation_en:
…benevolence extends universally to the myriad things and constitutes the heart of Heaven and Earth; the sage, through his heart, embodies the myriad things and thereby realizes benevolence. Thus, what under Heaven depends upon me is so weighty, yet I bear its burden; its reach is so distant, yet I travel its course. But this burden cannot be borne by physical strength, nor can this course be completed by footsteps. One must therefore root it in one’s own heart and embody it. Breadth and expansiveness are called magnanimity; strength and endurance are called resolve. But how do these relate to benevolence? Benevolence is precisely the heart. In its original condition, it is utterly still and free of desire. Without desire, its breadth, generosity, warmth, and gentleness suffice to accommodate all things, while its vigor, strength, firmness, and resolve suffice to hold fast. What is called the weighty burden and the distant course emerges from this. There is no separate benevolence outside this heart, no separate magnanimity and resolve outside benevolence, and no separate weighty burden and distant course outside magnanimity and resolve.
The human heart is originally vast, but bodily form and vital force fetter it. Once bodily form comes into being, many things enslave it; once awareness awakens, manifold things entice it. If these numerous and manifold desires fill the abode of receptive spiritual awareness, how could it fail to become small? Its magnanimity is indeed great, but thoughts of greed, rivalry, baseness, deceit, calculating cleverness, and selfishness enter and constrict it. Its resolve is indeed great, but habits of bending before gain [?], shrinking before authority, listlessness, and indolence enter and weaken it. Its weighty burden and distant course are indeed great, but the failings of narrowness, ignorance, neglect, and abandonment enter and obstruct them. Thus the gentleman examines himself to discern the slightest stirrings, disciplines himself to secure a return to his original condition, preserves sincerity to dispel delusion, and maintains reverent attentiveness to establish sincerity. Once constriction is removed, my magnanimity is naturally unimpaired; once weakness is removed, my resolve is naturally unimpaired; once obstruction is removed, my weighty burden and distant course…

title: 嘉靖三十一年陝西鄉試錄
text:
自如也卽因其本然之心以盡吾固有之性因
其固有之性以廣吾大同之仁本諸身則性情
理焉見諸事則禮樂光焉刑政憲焉施諸物則
品彙若焉徵諸民則元元惇惇遂焉參諸天地
則大順大化相爲官焉夫人物化也者盡性之
大也天地參焉者大之極也而君子之心視一
德之未脩曰吾之憂也視一物之未遂曰吾之
恫也視一民之未安曰吾之傷也視一災一沴
之未消曰吾之愆也不曰吾任是是巳舉矣吾
===
道是是巳及矣曰吾巳舉者有驕乎其心者也
驕則不可以爲弘曰吾巳及者有吝乎其心者
也吝則不可以爲毅故惟弘則有見於重而不
知其能舉也惟毅則有見於遠而不知其能及
也故曰仁以爲巳任不亦重乎死而後巳不亦
遠乎言心之無窮巳也必無窮巳而後可以爲
大心故性可盡也心不可滿也天可合也心不
可極也天垂象日月明四時序星辰行萬物昌
天之性誠盡矣維天之命於穆不巳則天之所
punctuated:
自如也。卽因其本然之心，以盡吾固有之性；因其固有之性，以廣吾大同之仁。本諸身，則性情理焉；見諸事，則禮樂光焉，刑政憲焉；施諸物，則品彙若焉；徵諸民，則元元惇惇遂焉；參諸天地，則大順大化相爲官焉。夫人物化也者，盡性之大也；天地參焉者，大之極也。而君子之心，視一德之未脩，曰：「吾之憂也。」視一物之未遂，曰：「吾之恫也。」視一民之未安，曰：「吾之傷也。」視一災一沴之未消，曰：「吾之愆也。」不曰：「吾任是，是巳舉矣；吾道是，是巳及矣。」

曰「吾巳舉」者，有驕乎其心者也；驕則不可以爲弘。曰「吾巳及」者，有吝乎其心者也；吝則不可以爲毅。故惟弘，則有見於重，而不知其能舉也；惟毅，則有見於遠，而不知其能及也。故曰：「仁以爲巳任，不亦重乎？死而後巳，不亦遠乎？」言心之無窮巳也。必無窮巳，而後可以爲大心。故性可盡也，心不可滿也；天可合也，心不可極也。

天垂象，日月明，四時序，星辰行，萬物昌，天之性誠盡矣。「維天之命，於穆不巳」，則天之所
translation_en:
…remains unimpeded. Thus, by following the heart in its original condition, I fully realize my inherent nature; by following that inherent nature, I extend my benevolence, which embraces all in unity. Rooted in oneself, it brings nature and feelings into order; manifested in affairs, it makes rites and music radiant, and punishments and government exemplary. Applied to things, it brings their various kinds into harmony; evidenced among the people, it enables the common people, in their sincerity, to flourish. Joining with Heaven and Earth, it participates with them in the work of supreme harmony and transformation. The transformation of people and things is the greatness of fully realizing nature; forming a triad with Heaven and Earth is the utmost extent of that greatness. Yet whenever the gentleman sees a single virtue left uncultivated, his heart says, “This is my concern.” When he sees a single thing that has not fulfilled its potential, he says, “This is my pain.” When he sees a single person not at peace, he says, “This is my sorrow.” When he sees a single calamity or baleful influence not yet dispelled, he says, “This is my fault.” He does not say, “This is my burden, and I have already borne it; this is my way, and I have already reached its end.”

One who says, “I have already borne it,” harbors pride in his heart; pride makes breadth of spirit impossible. One who says, “I have already reached it,” harbors narrowness in his heart; narrowness makes resolve impossible. Thus only with breadth of spirit does one recognize the weight of the burden without considering oneself capable of bearing it; only with resolve does one recognize the distance of the journey without considering oneself capable of reaching its end. Hence it is said: “Taking benevolence as one's own responsibility—is this not weighty? Ceasing only at death—is this not a long journey?” This speaks of the heart's knowing neither limit nor cessation. Only when it knows neither limit nor cessation can it be a great heart. Thus one's nature may be fully realized, but one's heart must never be complacent; one may unite with Heaven, but one's heart must never reach a limit.

Heaven displays its signs: the sun and moon shine, the four seasons follow their order, the stars move, and the myriad things flourish. Heaven's nature is indeed fully realized. Yet, “The mandate of Heaven—oh, how profound and unceasing!” This, then, is that by which Heaven…

title: 嘉靖三十一年陝西鄉試錄
text:
以爲天也堯舜垂衣而治由明德親民以至萬
邦協和四方風動光於日月格於上下聖人之
性有不盡哉然其愼脩思永者孳孳不少替也
則聖人之所以爲聖人者槩可知矣蓋於穆者
天之心孳孳者聖人之心天道高明帝德光大
高明者積之盛也光大者載之隆也觀其所積
載則天與聖人之弘毅一也故天任道而不已
聖人任仁而不已士者學爲聖人者也故求仁
於其重者遠者則不容不大其心求心於其大
===
者則不可以不弘毅程子曰弘而不毅則無規
矩而難立毅而不弘則隘陋而無以居之自下
學立心之始言也然其實則在察識仁體以廣
吾心而充之所謂寬以居之勇以行之者也聖
門之學以求仁爲要學者各得其資之所近故
子張才高意廣則失之難立子夏篤信謹守則
失之無以居之皆未知所以求仁曾子存誠而
有得焉故其說仁似夫子也大學言修齊治平
博矣而其道以絜矩施至於得失之際則歸之
punctuated: 以爲天也。堯舜垂衣而治，由明德親民，以至萬邦協和，四方風動，光於日月，格於上下，聖人之性有不盡哉？然其愼脩思永者，孳孳不少替也，則聖人之所以爲聖人者，槩可知矣。蓋於穆者，天之心；孳孳者，聖人之心。天道高明，帝德光大。高明者，積之盛也；光大者，載之隆也。觀其所積載，則天與聖人之弘毅一也。故天任道而不已，聖人任仁而不已。士者，學爲聖人者也。故求仁於其重者遠者，則不容不大其心；求心於其大者，則不可以不弘毅。程子曰：「弘而不毅，則無規矩而難立；毅而不弘，則隘陋而無以居之。」自下學立心之始言也。然其實則在察識仁體，以廣吾心而充之，所謂寬以居之、勇以行之者也。聖門之學，以求仁爲要。學者各得其資之所近，故子張才高意廣，則失之難立；子夏篤信謹守，則失之無以居之，皆未知所以求仁。曾子存誠而有得焉，故其說仁似夫子也。《大學》言修齊治平，博矣，而其道以絜矩施；至於得失之際，則歸之
translation_en: …is what makes Heaven Heaven. Yao and Shun let their robes hang down and the realm was governed. From manifesting luminous virtue and drawing close to the people, they brought the myriad states into harmony and moved the four quarters as though by the wind; their brilliance outshone the sun and moon, and their influence reached above and below. Was there any part of the sages’ nature that they did not fully realize? Yet in carefully cultivating themselves and taking thought for the enduring future, they labored diligently without the slightest slackening. From this we can broadly understand what makes sages sages. Profound unceasingness is Heaven’s heart; unremitting diligence is the sages’ heart. Heaven’s Way is lofty and luminous; the sage emperors’ virtue is radiant and great. Loftiness and luminosity are the fullness of accumulation; radiance and greatness are the abundance of what is borne. Observing what they accumulate and bear, we see that Heaven and the sages are one in breadth of spirit and steadfastness. Thus Heaven takes responsibility for the Way without ceasing, and the sages take responsibility for benevolence without ceasing. A scholar is one who learns to become a sage. Therefore, to seek benevolence as a heavy burden and a distant destination, one must enlarge one’s heart; to seek such largeness of heart, one must possess breadth of spirit and steadfastness. Master Cheng said: “With breadth of spirit but no steadfastness, one lacks rules and standards and finds it difficult to stand firm; with steadfastness but no breadth of spirit, one is narrow and confined and has no means of abiding in it.” This speaks from the standpoint of the beginning, when one establishes one’s resolve through elementary learning. In substance, however, it lies in discerning and recognizing the essential reality of benevolence, thereby broadening one’s heart and bringing it to fullness. This is what is meant by abiding in it with spaciousness and practicing it with courage. Learning in the school of the Sage takes the pursuit of benevolence as its essential task. Learners each attain what accords with their natural endowments. Thus Zizhang, with his lofty talents and expansive aspirations, erred in finding it difficult to stand firm; Zixia, with his firm faith and careful adherence, erred in lacking the means to abide in it. Neither yet understood how to seek benevolence. Zengzi preserved sincerity and attained an understanding of it; hence his account of benevolence resembled the Master’s. The Great Learning speaks of cultivating oneself, ordering the family, governing the state, and bringing peace to the world: its scope is broad indeed. Its Way is put into practice through the principle of the measuring square—judging one’s treatment of others by what one would wish for oneself. When it comes to the juncture between gaining and losing, however, it attributes these to…

title: 嘉靖三十一年陝西鄉試錄
text:
忠信與驕泰而天命之從違因之合弘毅而觀
之可也故君子知所以大心則知所以盡性知
所以盡性則知所以合天亦曰仁而已矣謹論
又
邢子深
同考試官教諭王〔皇賓〕批　此作發揮題義有開闔有變
化如明珠走盤恍無滯跡眞奇士矣
考試官教諭袁〔廷椿〕批　機軸不凡語意活潑
考試官教諭楊〔舉〕批　理精而文明
===
論曰道之在天下也至大也而具于人人惟充
其大也而道斯體之矣何也養也道之所由充
也不養則道也散失無紀無紀斯紊矣是故廣
愽者滯之淵微者塞之顯者晦之高者卑之蔽
之褻之窒之迫之淆而惑之震而懾之拂而抑
之蕩而不止隕墜而不能舉而君子任重道遠
之功荒矣故養斯急焉而有以容之而有以達
之弘毅焉爾矣惟弘則道之重者容之任之惟
毅則道之遠者達之致之而能事畢矣是故養
punctuated:
忠信與驕泰，而天命之從違因之。合弘毅而觀之，可也。故君子知所以大心，則知所以盡性；知所以盡性，則知所以合天。亦曰仁而已矣。謹論。
又
邢子深
同考試官教諭王〔皇賓〕批：此作發揮題義，有開闔，有變化，如明珠走盤，恍無滯跡，眞奇士矣。
考試官教諭袁〔廷椿〕批：機軸不凡，語意活潑。
考試官教諭楊〔舉〕批：理精而文明。
論曰：道之在天下也，至大也，而具于人人。惟充其大也，而道斯體之矣。何也？養也，道之所由充也。不養，則道也散失無紀；無紀，斯紊矣。是故廣愽者滯之，淵微者塞之，顯者晦之，高者卑之，蔽之，褻之，窒之，迫之，淆而惑之，震而懾之，拂而抑之，蕩而不止，隕墜而不能舉，而君子任重道遠之功荒矣。故養斯急焉，而有以容之，而有以達之，弘毅焉爾矣。惟弘，則道之重者容之、任之；惟毅，則道之遠者達之、致之，而能事畢矣。是故養
translation_en:
…loyalty and trustworthiness, on the one hand, and arrogance and self-indulgence, on the other; whether Heaven’s Mandate accords with or turns against one depends upon these. It is fitting to consider this in conjunction with broad-mindedness and resolution. Thus, when the gentleman knows how to enlarge his mind, he knows how to fulfill his nature; when he knows how to fulfill his nature, he knows how to accord with Heaven. This, too, is simply benevolence. Respectfully submitted as a discourse.

Another discourse
Xing Zishen

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang Huangbin, Instructor: This composition develops the meaning of the topic, opening out and drawing together, turning and transforming, like a bright pearl rolling on a tray, seemingly without a trace of impediment. Truly an exceptional talent!

Comment by Examiner Yuan Tingchun, Instructor: The conception is extraordinary, and the language and ideas are lively.

Comment by Examiner Yang Ju, Instructor: The reasoning is refined and the writing lucid.

The discourse says: The Way in the world is supremely great, yet it is present in every person. Only by fully developing its greatness can one embody the Way. How is this done? Through nurturing: this is how the Way is fully developed. Without nurturing, the Way becomes scattered and lost, without order; without order, there is confusion. Thus, what is broad and extensive is impeded; what is profound and subtle is obstructed; what is manifest is obscured; what is lofty is brought low. It is concealed, profaned, blocked, constrained, confused and confounded, shaken and intimidated, thwarted and suppressed. It drifts without stopping, falls and cannot be raised again; and the gentleman’s work of bearing a heavy burden along a distant course is neglected. Nurturing is therefore urgent. To have the capacity to contain it and the means to carry it through requires only broad-mindedness and resolution. Only through broad-mindedness can one contain and bear the weight of the Way; only through resolution can one traverse and attain its farthest reaches. Then all that one can accomplish is fulfilled. Therefore, nurturing…

title: 嘉靖三十一年陝西鄉試錄
text:
諸心者也心安而德滋嗚呼體仁之功至矣哉
雖然是非曾子之言也堯舜禹湯文武相傳之
心法也故于九德于六德曰寛曰剛曰義曰和
寛也和也弘也剛也義也毅也德之所以體而
行之也聖人授受之妙也吾常觀諸天地之所
以生萬物矣嫗煦覆育絪緼交通而有所謂物
所謂人焉所謂物物人人者焉而有所謂萬物
之物萬人之人者焉人也人人也者知之而不
養養之而不充者也而萬人之人斯士矣體仁
者也天下後世望而責焉者也其于物也同相
===
生也則同相感也同相感也則同相仁也而仁
之爲德廣矣君子之體仁非物物而育之事事
而卹之而渾淪磅礴之勢純粹惻怛之精天理
周流人欲不雜焉者自其心焉養之而已矣心
也所以具弘毅之本而弘毅焉者不能外心有
所容有所立焉者也自夫拘者狹其量不能容
而仁以偏惰者懈其守不能立而仁以廢物以
蔽之私以褻之忿以窒之勢以迫之愛惡以淆
punctuated:
諸心者也，心安而德滋。嗚呼！體仁之功至矣哉！雖然，是非曾子之言也，堯舜禹湯文武相傳之心法也。故于九德、于六德，曰寛、曰剛、曰義、曰和。寛也，和也，弘也；剛也，義也，毅也。德之所以體而行之也，聖人授受之妙也。
吾常觀諸天地之所以生萬物矣：嫗煦覆育，絪緼交通，而有所謂物、所謂人焉，所謂物物人人者焉，而有所謂萬物之物、萬人之人者焉。人也，人人也者，知之而不養，養之而不充者也；而萬人之人，斯士矣，體仁者也，天下後世望而責焉者也。其于物也，同相生也，則同相感也；同相感也，則同相仁也，而仁之爲德廣矣。
君子之體仁，非物物而育之，事事而卹之，而渾淪磅礴之勢、純粹惻怛之精，天理周流，人欲不雜焉者，自其心焉養之而已矣。心也，所以具弘毅之本，而弘毅焉者，不能外心有所容、有所立焉者也。自夫拘者狹其量，不能容，而仁以偏；惰者懈其守，不能立，而仁以廢。物以蔽之，私以褻之，忿以窒之，勢以迫之，愛惡以淆
translation_en:
…within the heart. When the heart is at peace, virtue flourishes. Ah! How consummate is the achievement of embodying benevolence! Nevertheless, these are not Zengzi’s words alone: they are the teaching of the heart transmitted successively by Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu. Thus, among the Nine Virtues and the Six Virtues are generosity, firmness, righteousness, and harmony. Generosity and harmony constitute broad-mindedness; firmness and righteousness constitute resolution. These are the means by which virtue is embodied and put into practice, the subtle essence of what the sages transmitted and received.
I have often contemplated how Heaven and Earth bring forth the myriad things. They warm and nurture, shelter and nourish; their vital forces intermingle and communicate. Thus there arise what we call things and what we call human beings; there are those that fulfill their nature as things and those who fulfill their nature as human beings [?]; and there are things that stand for all things and persons who stand for all people [?]. Those who are human, and those who fulfill their humanity [?], may understand this without nurturing it, or nurture it without bringing it to fullness. But the person who stands for all people is the scholar: one who embodies benevolence, upon whom the world and later generations place their expectations and demands. In relation to other beings, sharing in the same process of generation means responding to one another; responding to one another means exercising benevolence toward one another. Broad indeed, then, is benevolence as a virtue!
The gentleman’s embodiment of benevolence does not consist in nourishing each thing individually or attending solicitously to each separate affair. Rather, he need only nurture within his own heart that all-embracing, expansive power and that pure essence of compassion, in which heavenly principle circulates throughout, unmixed with human desires. The heart contains the foundation of broad-mindedness and resolution. Those who possess these qualities cannot find their capacity to embrace things or to stand firm outside the heart. The constrained narrow their capacity and cannot embrace things, so their benevolence becomes partial; the indolent relax their vigilance and cannot stand firm, so their benevolence falls into disuse. External things obscure it; selfishness defiles it; anger obstructs it; circumstances oppress it; likes and dislikes confuse…

title: 嘉靖三十一年陝西鄉試錄
text:
惑之利害以震慴之事變以拂抑之滯其廣慱
塞其淵微晦其顯者卑其高者而仁之重且遠
者斯莫之體矣是故曾子之所以憂也而于天
德致意焉曰弘毅而已矣弘毅非由外鑠也士
之所以養其心以達天地之全也曰仁也一弘
毅也非弘毅之外而別有所謂仁也寬裕溫柔
仁之有容也而弘矣發强剛毅仁之有執也而
毅矣仁非弘毅無以體而毅而非弘弘而非毅
偏焉而已矣而烏足以語仁是故性之德也合
===
一之道也而天地盡之矣故乾知大始非弘乎
運行不息非毅乎坤作成物非弘乎承天時行
非毅乎天地之道也人善反之而天地之理存
焉者也吾見廣大而不竭强幹而不撓兼衆善
而不繁納萬有而不隘包括乎造化而不盈特
立乎風流而不靡貞之以至一之性確之以至
堅之守而凡物之可喜可虞可疾可懼可驚可
愕者錯雜于前而不動而仁之所以體者至矣
是故德之元也吾其運之善之長也吾其復之
punctuated: 惑之，利害以震慴之，事變以拂抑之，滯其廣慱，塞其淵微，晦其顯者，卑其高者，而仁之重且遠者，斯莫之體矣。是故曾子之所以憂也，而于天德致意焉，曰弘毅而已矣。弘毅非由外鑠也，士之所以養其心，以達天地之全也。曰仁也，一弘毅也，非弘毅之外而別有所謂仁也。寬裕溫柔，仁之有容也，而弘矣；發强剛毅，仁之有執也，而毅矣。仁非弘毅無以體，而毅而非弘，弘而非毅，偏焉而已矣，而烏足以語仁？是故性之德也，合一之道也，而天地盡之矣。故乾知大始，非弘乎？運行不息，非毅乎？坤作成物，非弘乎？承天時行，非毅乎？天地之道也，人善反之，而天地之理存焉者也。吾見廣大而不竭，强幹而不撓，兼衆善而不繁，納萬有而不隘，包括乎造化而不盈，特立乎風流而不靡，貞之以至一之性，確之以至堅之守，而凡物之可喜、可虞、可疾、可懼、可驚、可愕者，錯雜于前而不動，而仁之所以體者至矣。是故德之元也，吾其運之；善之長也，吾其復之。
translation_en: …confuse it; advantage and harm frighten it; changing circumstances thwart and oppress it. They obstruct its breadth [?], block its profound subtlety, obscure what is manifest in it, and abase what is lofty in it. Thus no one can embody benevolence, with its weighty burden and far-reaching course. This is what troubled Zengzi. Turning his attention to Heaven’s virtue, he spoke simply of breadth of spirit and firmness of resolve. These are not infused from outside: they are the means by which a scholar nourishes his mind and attains the wholeness of Heaven and Earth. What we call benevolence is entirely this breadth and firmness; there is no separate thing called benevolence beyond them. Generosity, tolerance, gentleness, and tenderness constitute benevolence’s capacity to accommodate, and thus its breadth. Vigor, strength, steadfastness, and resolution constitute benevolence’s capacity to hold fast, and thus its firmness. Without breadth and firmness, benevolence cannot be embodied. Yet firmness without breadth, or breadth without firmness, is merely one-sided. How could that suffice for speaking of benevolence? Thus the virtue of our nature is a Way that unites these as one, and Heaven and Earth exemplify it fully. Qian, the Creative, presides over the great beginning: is this not breadth? Its movement never ceases: is this not firmness? Kun, the Receptive, brings things to completion: is this not breadth? It follows Heaven and acts according to the seasons: is this not firmness? Such is the Way of Heaven and Earth. When people successfully return to it, the principles of Heaven and Earth abide within them. I see one who is expansive without exhaustion, strong in his core without yielding, embracing all goodness without becoming encumbered, and accommodating all existence without being confined; encompassing creation without becoming overfull, standing independently amid prevailing currents without being swept along. He makes this upright through a nature of utmost unity and secures it through a commitment of utmost firmness. Whatever may delight, trouble, disgust, frighten, startle, or astonish him may appear before him in bewildering profusion, yet he remains unmoved. The embodiment of benevolence thereby reaches its utmost realization. Thus, as benevolence is the originating power of virtue, let me put it into operation; as it is the foremost of all goodness, let me return to it…

title: 嘉靖三十一年陝西鄉試錄
text:
包四德者吾其栝之統百行者吾其蓄之渾淪
磅礴者吾其充裕之純粹惻怛者吾其蹈諳之
勿物以蔽之勿私以藥之勿忿以窒之勿勢以
迫之勿愛惡以淆惑之勿利害以震懾之勿事
變以拂抑之廣愽者勿滯之淵微者勿塞之顯
者勿晦之高者勿卑之可以還天地之元可以
復萬物之始可以踐形惟肖可以視履無虧其
遠也可任其重也可致斯之謂父母之宗子而
參賛化育出入古今對越上帝幽賛神明同天
===
地之貞觀合日月之貞明盡人道之貞勝不依
形而立不恃勢而存不待通而行不隨塞而亡
物化而道不置身逝而理俱恒斯反之心而無
歉矣吁是道也何道也聖人傳授之心法也聖
斯至矣賢其次焉而士也者由賢以希聖者也
百姓無與焉者也而後世異端者出煦煦爲仁
弘也蔽矣子子爲義毅也荒矣而兼愛之弊其
下若子之仁遠矣夷之隘也惠之和也愿之恪
也根之剛也似弘毅而非弘毅者也道其道而
punctuated:
包四德者，吾其栝之；統百行者，吾其蓄之；渾淪磅礴者，吾其充裕之；純粹惻怛者，吾其蹈諳之。勿物以蔽之，勿私以藥之，勿忿以窒之，勿勢以迫之，勿愛惡以淆惑之，勿利害以震懾之，勿事變以拂抑之。廣愽者勿滯之，淵微者勿塞之，顯者勿晦之，高者勿卑之。可以還天地之元，可以復萬物之始，可以踐形惟肖，可以視履無虧。其遠也可任，其重也可致。斯之謂父母之宗子，而參賛化育，出入古今，對越上帝，幽賛神明，同天地之貞觀，合日月之貞明，盡人道之貞勝。不依形而立，不恃勢而存，不待通而行，不隨塞而亡。物化而道不置，身逝而理俱恒，斯反之心而無歉矣。
吁！是道也，何道也？聖人傳授之心法也。聖斯至矣，賢其次焉，而士也者，由賢以希聖者也，百姓無與焉者也。而後世異端者出，煦煦爲仁，弘也蔽矣；子子爲義，毅也荒矣。而兼愛之弊，其下若子之仁遠矣。夷之隘也，惠之和也，愿之恪也，根之剛也，似弘毅而非弘毅者也。道其道而
translation_en:
…That which embraces the four virtues, I shall gather together; that which unites the hundred forms of conduct, I shall store up. That which is whole and boundlessly expansive, I shall bring to fullness; that which is pure and compassionately concerned, I shall practice and comprehend. Do not let external things obscure it, selfishness poison it [?], anger obstruct it, or power constrain it. Do not let love and hatred confuse it, benefit and harm intimidate it, or changing circumstances frustrate and suppress it. Do not impede its breadth, block its profound subtlety, darken its clarity, or abase its loftiness. Thus one can return to the primal source of Heaven and Earth and recover the beginning of the myriad things; one can fulfill the endowment of one’s bodily form and truly resemble its source, and scrutinize one’s conduct and find it without flaw. However distant the journey, one can undertake it; however heavy the burden, one can carry it to its destination. This is what it means to be the principal heir of one’s parents: to assist in transformation and nurture, to move through past and present, to stand reverently before the Lord on High, and to assist unseen the spiritual powers. One shares the constancy displayed by Heaven and Earth, accords with the constant brightness of the sun and moon, and fully realizes the power of constancy to prevail in the human Way. One stands without depending on physical form, endures without relying on power, acts without awaiting favorable circumstances, and does not perish when obstructed. Things change, yet the Way is not abandoned; the body passes away, yet principle abides forever. Reflecting upon this in one’s heart, one has nothing to regret.
Ah! What Way is this? It is the teaching of the mind transmitted by the sages. Sages attain its utmost reach; worthies stand next to them. Scholars aspire to sagehood by way of worthiness; the common people have no part in this. Yet in later ages heterodox teachings arose. They took petty kindness for benevolence, obscuring breadth of spirit; they took “zi zi” [?] for righteousness, neglecting resolute strength. As for the faults of indiscriminate love, it falls far below the benevolence of Ruozi [?]. Yi’s narrowness, Hui’s accommodating temper, the punctiliousness of the conventionally upright, and Gen’s rigidity [?] resemble breadth and resolution but are not truly breadth and resolution. They follow their own way, yet…

title: 嘉靖三十一年陝西鄉試錄
text:
非聖賢之所謂中道也蔽之窒之迫之濟
惑之震懾之拂抑之之所由起也曾子謂弘毅
求仁者教天下者也善乎顏氏之子乎不遷怒
不貳過弘毅備之矣而夫子實楹參也易簀其
達任重道遠之義乎宰我之從魯子貢之說齊
半塗而廢焉嗚呼是未究弘毅之說者敝也〻〻
矣吁安得弘毅之士出而與之語體仁之功哉
謹論
表
擬宋以左諫議大夫陳恕爲河北東路招
置營田使謝表〔端拱二年〕
王埠

非聖賢之所謂中道也。蔽之、窒之、迫之、濟惑之、震懾之、拂抑之之所由起也。曾子謂弘毅，求仁者、教天下者也。善乎顏氏之子乎！不遷怒，不貳過，弘毅備之矣。而夫子實楹參也，易簀，其達任重道遠之義乎？宰我之從魯，子貢之說齊，半塗而廢焉。嗚呼！是未究弘毅之說者敝也〻〻矣。吁！安得弘毅之士出而與之語體仁之功哉！謹論。

translation_en:
…is not the Way of the Mean spoken of by the sages and worthies. This is the source of obstruction, blockage, constraint, compounded confusion [?], intimidation, and suppression. Zengzi’s words about breadth of spirit and resolve were intended for those seeking benevolence and for instructing all under Heaven. Admirable indeed was the son of the Yan family! He did not transfer his anger to others or repeat his faults: breadth of spirit and resolve were fully present in him. And the Master indeed [an unclear statement concerning Zeng Shen; ?]. In having his sleeping mat changed before his death, did Zeng Shen not comprehend the meaning of “the burden is heavy and the road is long”? Zai Wo’s following Lu [?] and Zigong’s persuasion of Qi amounted to abandoning the journey halfway. Alas! Such is the failing of those who have not thoroughly understood the teaching of breadth of spirit and resolve—the text repeats its lament here [?]. Ah! Where might one find a man of such breadth and resolve with whom to discuss the work of embodying benevolence? Respectfully submitted as a discourse.

Memorial

Its diction, moreover, is brilliant; reading it moves the heart. For these reasons it has been selected〕 as a model.
